name: v0.10.0
body:
This release replaces the Go implementation of many-ai-cli with a Rust one.

- **Same commands, same places for your data.** The command names, settings and
  data locations are unchanged: the configuration stays in
  `~/.many-ai-cli/config.yaml` and your data under `~/.many-ai-cli/`. Updating
  carries over your settings and your session list (sessions older than the
  retention period are removed at each start, as in v0.9.0). The text of past
  conversations is not carried over: this version no longer stores it, and the
  first start after the update deletes what v0.9.0 saved (see "Changed").
- **Going back.** Before updating, copy `~/.many-ai-cli/`. To return to the Go
  version, reinstall v0.9.0 and write the copy back. Steps:
  [Upgrading to 0.10 (Rust)](https://github.com/ishizakahiroshi/many-ai-cli#upgrading-to-010-rust).
- **No official Docker image.** Official Docker images, container builds and
  automatic updates are not part of v0.10.0, and automatic image publishing is
  stopped (see `deploy/docker/README.md`). Use the Linux binary instead.
- **Known limitations.** Starting an AI CLI session usually shows its first
  output in well under a second, but now and then it takes two to four seconds
  (measured on one machine over 24 launches: median 0.34 s, 95th percentile
  0.9 s, slowest 4.0 s). The cause has not been found.

### Fixed

- **Finished work is no longer reported as failed because of a word in its
  details.** A summary was marked "failed" (board label, high-priority
  notification) whenever it contained 失敗, エラー, failed or error anywhere, so
  reports such as "fixed the test that failed 2 of 3 runs" or "0 errors" went
  out as failures. "Failed" and "stopped" are now read from how the first
  sentence ends: text in parentheses, "none found" phrases (失敗 0 件, no
  errors) and the earlier clauses of a listing are left out. A first sentence
  that says the work is unfinished (未完了) counts as failed. A wait for your
  decision is still recognised anywhere in the summary.
- **A file path that a CLI breaks across two lines opens as one link
  again.** Some CLIs (Codex's bulleted lists, for example) end a line on a
  directory and continue the path on the next line with a few spaces of
  indent. The terminal then linked only the first half of the path, so the
  preview and "open in app" actions failed. The indent is now ignored when it
  follows a path separator or is two or more spaces wide.
- **Codex sessions started with a subscription profile can use the Codex
  Desktop browser plugins.** Codex Desktop installs its Browser and Chrome
  plugins only into your default Codex home, and Codex ignores them in a
  profile, so asking a profile session to operate Chrome stopped before it
  connected. When Codex Desktop is installed, preparing a Codex profile now
  links the profile to Desktop's bundled plugins and installs the two plugins
  into it with `codex plugin add` (once; later launches only check that they
  are there). A failed install is reported with the other profile notices and
  is tried again next time. Nothing changes without Codex Desktop.
- **Saving a file no longer fails for a moment while the Hub starts a
  process.** A child process can briefly hold the lock of a file a save just
  closed, and a save in that moment was refused as "being saved by another
  process".
  The save now tries the lock again for up to about 40 ms before refusing.
- **Review and commit details show each file's own diff.** A file name was
  passed to Git as a pattern, so the diff for `a[b].txt` also carried the
  changes of `ab.txt`, and a name Git quotes (one with a control character)
  showed "(no diff)". Each file is now matched by its exact name, and file
  names and line counts are read in Git's NUL-separated form.
- **`many-ai-cli stop` no longer ends a program that was given the Hub's old
  PID.** A Hub that ended without cleaning up (its console closed, a sign-out,
  a crash) left its PID in `hub-runtime.json`. Once the system gave that PID to
  another program, `stop` force-ended that program, and a new Hub refused to
  start while it ran. The record now also keeps the Hub process's identity
  (its creation time, plus the boot on Linux). `stop` checks it on the same
  process handle it ends, leaves a program that only holds the PID running and
  removes the stale record, and startup no longer counts that program as a
  Hub. Records written by earlier versions are judged by whether the process
  already existed when the record was written. On macOS, where a process
  cannot be identified this way, a Hub that does not answer the stop request
  is no longer force-ended: `stop` says so and leaves it to you.
- **Saving a file from the Hub no longer leaves it half written.** The editor
  wrote the new text over the file in place, so a full disk, an I/O error or
  the Hub stopping partway could leave the start of the new text followed by
  the end of the old one. The earlier content is now copied to
  `~/.many-ai-cli/tmp/save-backups` first and put back if the write fails;
  the copy is removed once the save is complete. If a save is interrupted the
  copy stays there for 7 days. The file is still written in place, so its
  links and permissions are unchanged.
- **A child started again after a timeout keeps its depth.** With
  `orchestration.max_depth` above 1 and `timeout_respawn` on, a child that
  timed out at depth 2 was started again at depth 1, so it could start
  children deeper than `max_depth` allows. The replacement now has the depth
  of the child it replaces.
- **`setup` and `uninstall --purge` handle typographic apostrophes in paths
  on Windows.** A path containing ‘ ’ ‚ or ‛ (in a user name, or in a
  OneDrive folder named after an organization) ended the PowerShell string
  early, so the shortcuts were not created and `uninstall --purge` reported
  success without removing the program. These quotes are now doubled like
  the ASCII one.
- **`doctor` reports the size of the log directory again.** Once the Hub had
  started a session, the log directory held subdirectories (`spawn/`,
  `sessions/`), and `doctor` always warned that it could not check the size
  and told you to check the read permission. Subdirectories are now counted;
  links are still not followed.
- **`doctor` checks the permissions of `config.yaml` and `~/.many-ai-cli` on
  Windows.** It said it had checked them without reading them. It now warns
  when anyone other than you, SYSTEM and Administrators is allowed in, or when
  the file takes its permissions from the parent folder.
- **The Hub no longer writes past a buffer when it reads a Git process's
  command line on Windows.** A process named `git.exe` that set an odd length
  on its own command line made the Hub write one byte beyond the buffer. Such
  a process is now treated as unreadable, so a lock it may hold is not
  removed.
- **Routine history stays bounded.** Every run was kept forever, the whole
  history was copied every 2 seconds and rewritten on every change, so a
  routine used for months made the Hub slower. Each routine now keeps its
  newest 200 ended runs (the most the run list shows) plus any run in
  progress; older runs and their request records are removed, and an older
  file is trimmed when the Hub starts. The 2-second check now copies only the
  runs in progress.
- **A long line without spaces no longer freezes the chat view.** Finding file
  paths in a reply took time that grew with the square of the line length, so
  a reply with a long hexadecimal string could stop the whole dashboard,
  approval buttons included, for seconds. Relative paths are now matched up to
  255 characters (longer ones still link when they start with `./` or `/`).
- **A save the Hub was stopped in the middle of is now reported, and the
  earlier content can be put back.** Saving in the Files tab keeps a copy of
  the file's earlier content until the new content is written. If the Hub was
  killed or the machine lost power during the write, the file stayed half
  written and the copy stayed under a random name with nothing saying which
  file it belonged to; nobody was told, and a later save deleted copies older
  than seven days. Each copy now carries a record of its file, time and size.
  When you open the dashboard, a notice lists such files with two buttons: put
  the earlier content back, or delete the copy. A copy is removed by age only
  seven days after it was first listed for you. Copies left by earlier
  versions are listed without a file name and can be deleted from the notice.
- **A provider's own flags no longer cut off the options that follow them at
  launch.** The wrapper reads its own flags and stops at the first one it does
  not know. A custom provider's model arguments (`model_args` other than
  `--model <name>`) and an effort mapping written in the provider's own flags
  (Codex's `-c model_reasoning_effort="…"`, a custom `effort_args`) were placed
  before the wrapper's remaining flags, so the first prompt, the allowed tools,
  headless mode and the UTF-8 setting that followed could be handed to the
  provider as arguments instead of being applied. These arguments are now
  passed last, after `--`.
- **Starting a Codex session no longer waits for its browser plugins to be
  installed.** The first start of a Codex profile ran `codex plugin add` for
  the bundled browser plugins and waited for it, up to the command's time
  limit, on every start while the install kept failing (for example without a
  network). The install now runs in the background: the session starts at
  once, the notice says the plugins are being installed, a failure is reported
  on the next start, and a failed install is tried again after 30 minutes.
- **A suggested commit message weighs a new file by its own size when the
  session works in a subfolder.** Untracked files are named from the
  repository root, but their line counts were read relative to the session's
  folder, so in a subfolder the count was 0 or that of another file with the
  same relative name.
- **A message with a very long run of spaces or blank lines no longer freezes
  the dashboard.** Every received chat message is tidied (trailing spaces,
  leading and trailing blank lines) whether or not the chat view is open. A
  single line of 200,000 spaces followed by a character, or as many blank
  lines inside a code block, took about 11 seconds each in V8 (the JavaScript
  engine of Chrome; measured with Node), during which the page does not
  respond. The same inputs now take under 20 milliseconds; the tidied text is
  unchanged.
- Fix the Workflow progress display while a background Workflow runs: it no longer
  reads the "Update installed" notice as a finished agent (which showed 1/1 and
  100%), shows the real count from the Workflow journal instead, and the
  "not progressing" warning is no longer shown while a background Workflow is
  still running.
- Fix Windows terminal disposal during process startup: terminate the owned Job
  and observe the root exit and an empty Job before closing ConPTY, preventing
  startup-close initialization errors. Ctrl+C input remains a separate operation.
- Shell attachment destinations can specify an SSH private key file for uploads,
  downloads, and remote file previews, including keys passed with `ssh -i` when
  connecting in the terminal.
- Keep all long pasted texts before sending, and retain the draft when an
  attachment upload fails instead of sending an incomplete message.

- **The retention settings take effect again.** `log.session_retention_days`
  (default 7), `handoff.retention_days` (14) and `log.attachment_retention_days`
  (7) were never read, so old session files, handoff records, history rows and
  attachments stayed forever. The Hub now applies them once at each start;
  zero or less keeps everything. Attachments wait one retention period after
  the first start with this version, so nothing you attached earlier is removed
  all at once.
- **Secrets saved before the masking was added are masked on the next start.**
  Existing `.log` files are masked once as a whole (so a key split across reads
  or a multi-line private key is caught), and approval texts already in the
  database are masked in place.
- **The handoff directory no longer grows by repeating the same transcript path.**
  A record was appended every time the transcript file changed, although the
  path rarely did (133 MB of a 145 MB directory in one install). A path equal to
  the previous one is skipped, and the Hub start folds the repeats already
  written; the handoff note shows the same content.
- **Sending an attachment from a shell session with no destination chosen now
  asks first.** Images, files and long pastes used to be sent silently with a
  path on this PC, which an AI running on the ssh machine could not open. A
  window now appears before sending: enter the ssh destination and press Save,
  or press "Read on this PC". Your input and attachments are kept.
- **A session's dedicated worktree is removed once its branch is merged on the
  remote, and one left behind is checked again at the next Hub start.** With
  `worktree_cleanup: delete`, closing a session now also fetches the upstream of
  the repository's current branch (`HEAD@{upstream}`, e.g. `origin/develop`) and
  counts the branch as merged when it is there, not only in the local HEAD; a
  worktree still unmerged when its session closed is judged again each time the
  Hub starts, skipping any a running session uses. An unreachable remote keeps
  the worktree and logs a warning, and the branch is never deleted. A squash or
  rebase merge on GitHub creates new commits, so it is not recognized as merged.
- **Commands an AI runs no longer write color codes into pipes and files.**
  With "Always show colors (recommended)", sessions received `FORCE_COLOR=3`
  and `CLICOLOR_FORCE=1`, and the AI CLI passes its environment to every
  command it runs, so `gh … --json`, test runners and other tools colored
  their output even when it was piped (JSON from `gh` could not be parsed).
  The setting now removes inherited `NO_COLOR`, `FORCE_COLOR`,
  `CLICOLOR_FORCE` and `CLICOLOR` instead and leaves color detection to the
  terminal pane, which still reports `TERM=xterm-256color` and
  `COLORTERM=truecolor`. "Follow the launch environment" and "No colors" are
  unchanged. Applies to newly started sessions.

- Approval rules now reach instruction files you reach through a link, such as
  a worktree or profile folder that is a junction or symlink, or a `CLAUDE.md`
  symlinked from your dotfiles. As in v0.9.0, the rules are written to the file
  the link points to, and two profiles linking one file keep the rules until
  the last of their sessions ends. Earlier Rust candidate builds silently gave these
  sessions no rules, so their AI could not offer choices as dashboard buttons. Trial runs
  still refuse links. `many-ai-cli doctor` (and Settings → doctor) now names
  live sessions whose instruction file is missing the rules.
- The ↑ up / ↓ down buttons that jump to the start or the end of a full-screen
  (alternate-screen) CLI's history no longer stop partway. They now send four
  scroll steps at a time instead of waiting for each step to be confirmed on
  screen, and treat the edge as reached once the visible text stops changing.
- Updated Tokio to 1.53.3 and the Web Push P-256 dependency to 0.14.0,
  including crypto-bigint 0.7.8 and ctutils 0.4.5 security fixes. Unix PTY I/O
  now explicitly registers its owned file descriptor under Tokio's lifetime
  contract; Web Push retains its encryption and signature wire formats.
- Windows file operations now hold the parent directory against replacement
  before opening the selected file, preventing a renamed parent from redirecting
  that open to a different file.
- One-tap approval links now bind the session's incarnation as well as its
  approval identity, so a link issued before a session is recreated cannot
  approve the replacement. Normal wrapper reconnects retain valid links;
  older token formats are rejected.
- Updated vendored DOMPurify to 3.4.17, retaining upstream license terms and
  matching the version shown in About and the frontend dependency list.
- Updated the TLS verifier and bundled root certificate dependencies to
  rustls-webpki 0.103.16 and webpki-root-certs 1.0.10, and pinned CI job Node.js
  to the 22.23.4 security release with native-build version receipts.
- Live status colors now follow the light or dark theme by default, with separate
  background and text overrides for each mode. The palette shows the mode being
  edited and can reset it without changing the other mode; legacy shared colors
  remain available in dark mode only.
- Remote browser connections now expire with their PIN session and disconnect
  on logout or PIN changes. New input and UI data are rejected after revocation;
  already accepted input drains while local screens and terminal sessions stay
  connected. Failed PIN persistence keeps existing connections authorized.
- Subscription probe and login cleanup now rechecks the exact session connection
  while dismissing it, so cleanup from an older connection cannot remove a
  reconnected session or emit a duplicate dismissal after removal.
- Cancelling uninstall, closing its input, or failing to read confirmation now
  leaves the running Hub untouched. Hub shutdown and data removal begin only
  after explicit confirmation.
- Windows release resource validation accepts the SDK's zero-to-one icon-plane
  normalization while still requiring matching icon image bytes, directory
  fields, image count, file version, and product version.
- npm packages and Linux package documentation now retain the Web dependency
  license notices from the canonical release ZIPs. Packaging rejects missing,
  empty, or inconsistent Web notices before replacing any output.
- Debug builds no longer collect temporary UI-freeze recorder events. Existing
  diagnostic files are preserved; the underlying investigation remains open.
- Windows desktop shortcuts now open the Hub and browser on the first launch,
  while sign-in starts only the tray. Setup retains the selected home and port;
  tray startup/action failures are shown instead of disappearing with the console.
- npm staging checks all four native inputs before replacing package payloads
  and verifies copied hashes. Package smoke checks require the correct Windows
  executable name and nonempty binaries instead of accepting missing payloads.
- In light mode, the footer and its detail panels now follow the light theme, <!-- doxguard: allow panel -->
  and the live status bar refreshes its saved colors after preference sync.
- The inline Usage meter now gives its remaining-quota bar the width left after
  its value and reset text, so the fill is easier to read on narrow rows.
- An approval question that the AI wrote without numbered options or
  `(Y:1/N:0)` (for example a single "May I push this?") is now shown as a
  Yes / No panel instead of the "corrupted structure" notice, and a plain report <!-- doxguard: allow panel -->
  wrapped in the approval marker no longer leaves the session waiting for
  approval. When the screen still cannot read an approval, the notice no longer
  blames a terminal redraw.

- The Git panel's read-only views (changed files, diffs and the commit-message <!-- doxguard: allow panel -->
  suggestion) no longer take `.git/index.lock`. They now run `git status` with
  `GIT_OPTIONAL_LOCKS=0` and compare HEAD with the work tree through
  `git diff-index`, which never rewrites the index, so a read stopped at its
  5-second limit can no longer leave a 0-byte `index.lock` that blocks your own
  `git add` / `git commit`. Commit, push, pull and fetch are unchanged.
- Session cards read the branch name from the repository's `.git/HEAD` file
  instead of starting `git` for it on every refresh. Starting `git` sometimes
  took longer than the 250 ms limit when many sessions were open, and the card
  then showed "(no git)" for a repository. Git is still asked when HEAD is
  detached, when the repository uses reftable, or when HEAD cannot be read. A
  repository with no commit yet now shows its branch name instead of
  "(no git)".
- Relay's change count and the clean check before an automatic worktree is
  removed no longer take `.git/index.lock` either: they ran `git status` without
  `GIT_OPTIONAL_LOCKS=0` and are stopped after 3 and 5 seconds. Every `git` the
  Hub starts (the Git panel, the branch display, relay, worktrees, turn records, <!-- doxguard: allow panel -->
  the approval-rule location and `doctor`) is now planned in one place that
  sets `GIT_OPTIONAL_LOCKS=0` and refuses a porcelain `git diff` against the
  work tree, and a test fails when new code starts `git` without it.
- Rust Hub keeps Codex sessions running through silent processing until the provider reports completion or interruption, and restores active turns outside the chat-history window after reconnection, preventing premature yellow unread-stop marks.
- The Windows Hub no longer builds a machine-wide thread snapshot every time it
  starts a child process (for example each `git` call that refreshes the branch
  display), which took more than half of the Hub's CPU. It now looks only at the
  child it just started, and releases that snapshot correctly so Hub handles do
  not accumulate.
- `orchestrate spawn` for a role that already has a live child is refused
  right away with the existing 409, before the spawn confirmation dialog opens.
  Previously the dialog opened, and the refusal came only after the user had
  chosen options and approved. `--force` still opens the dialog.
- Approval confirmations and mobile hold controls stay attached to the approval
  originally displayed. Enter activates the focused confirmation button.
  Read-only Markdown removes interactive controls, and browser policy blocks
  native form submission.
- Sending text, preparing attachments and completing voice input retain the
  originating session and preserve newer drafts when asynchronous work finishes.
- Windows terminal fallback passes its directory as data. Headless argument
  prompts require a native executable or a provider with stdin prompt transport
  when an unresolved Windows command shim would otherwise interpret the prompt.
  Trial CLI updates validate the executable selected after shim resolution.
- Instruction injection records cleanup intent before changing user files.
  Probe recovery checks identity captured from the owned process at startup;
  older or unverifiable records are retained with a warning for manual recovery.
- The Rust TLS dependency resolves to rustls 0.23.46.
- Web Push signs a normalized origin and a single contact URI. Unauthenticated
  WebSockets have a bounded wait and connection count. Concurrent in-app file
  saves report a conflict, and attachments rejected before journal acceptance
  remove only the newly created file.
- Files previews discard superseded responses and keep saves attached to the
  file and editor that started them. Git and Review tabs only reconnect to a
  matching repository, including when restoring tabs after a restart.
- History viewers discard results from closed or replaced views. Completing
  an earlier AI icon upload preserves a newly opened provider form. Memo editors
  keep IME conversion Enter separate from submitting or saving text.
- SVG files use external-open or download actions instead of an unsupported
  in-app image preview.
- **Editing a minified dependency no longer marks its unchanged text as a new
  secret.** Staged scans retain the baseline only for occurrences entirely in
  identical parts of a single-line replacement; new occurrences still block.
- **Terminal text no longer blurs at browser zoom levels other than 100%.** At
  zoom levels such as 90%, the terminal could draw every row slightly stretched,
  so text looked smeared until the layout changed again (for example when a bar
  above or below the terminal appeared or disappeared). The bundled xterm.js
  WebGL addon (0.19.0) now carries the upstream fix
  ([xtermjs/xterm.js#5607](https://github.com/xtermjs/xterm.js/pull/5607)), so
  rows are always drawn at their exact pixel height.
- Rust Hub attachment uploads now record history with the current session binding,
  fixing HTTP 500 failures that prevented images and pasted text from reaching the
  provider. WebSocket attachments also reject ended or stale session contexts.
- Hide unfinished completion tags when a terminal redraw interrupts them, while
  preserving cursor movement and the following output in the Rust trial UI.
- **The Settings icon stays at the bottom while Settings is open.** The same
  Settings, Usage and Hub buttons remain available, and the settings list can
  scroll past them.
- **Pasting into the work memo and other text fields stays in that field.**
  Pasting five or more lines (or more than 300 characters) into the memo box,
  the file editor, the commit message or any other text field turned the text
  into a "Pasted text" chip on the input bar at the bottom instead, and an
  image pasted into the memo box was also added to the input bar's
  attachments. The input bar now collects only pastes aimed at itself or at no
  text field.
- **The Detached Grid launcher shows readable labels again.** Its title,
  presets and buttons were shown as raw translation keys such as `dgl_title`.
- **Renaming a session card no longer breaks routine completion tracking or
  reattach matching.** The Hub now keys those lookups on a fixed launch-time
  label instead of the editable display label. The card's right-click "Change
  label" now opens an input dialog matching the New Session label field
  (translated menu text, current value pre-filled, blank clears back to the
  automatic title) instead of a plain browser prompt, and detached/Grid pane
  headings pick up the new name immediately.
- **Handoff allows continuing with the same CLI**, including Codex-to-Codex.
  The source CLI is no longer omitted from the destination picker; launching
  the successor and choosing a subscription remain explicit user actions.
- **Hub restarts preserve input sequence numbers and the full 2 MiB replay
  window from updated wrappers.** New instructions are no longer discarded as
  duplicate input after reconnect, and retained terminal history is no longer
  reduced to 64 KiB. Already discarded output cannot be recovered by this fix.
- **Terminal link detection avoids repeated full scans on long output.** URL
  suffixes with many unmatched brackets and Windows paths with long whitespace
  runs are processed in linear passes. Rows containing many links use a compact
  occupancy map and binary row lookup instead of scanning every earlier link
  and row, preserving link priority, targets and clickable ranges.
- **The prompt template picker is larger, and the mouse wheel now scrolls its
  list.** The picker opens wider and taller, and scrolling the wheel over it
  scrolls the list instead of the terminal behind it.
- **Files API endpoints protect repository roots and version control directories (.git, .hg, .svn).**
  Deleting, renaming, moving, creating, or editing paths within or targeting
  version control directories and root directories is rejected with 403 Forbidden
  or 409 Conflict.
- **Approval risk classification recognizes PowerShell array subexpressions `@(...)`.**
  Commands that embed arbitrary PowerShell statements via `@(...)` (such as
  `cat @(...)` or `dir @(...)`) are classified as mid-risk instead of incorrectly
  being treated as low-risk.
- **Web UI requests use Cookie and Bearer authorization instead of query tokens.**
  API calls across the web dashboard no longer include `?token=` in request URLs,
  preventing token exposure in browser history, server access logs, and shared links.
- **Dependency `golang.org/x/crypto` updated to v0.57.0**, eliminating upstream advisory GO-2025-3486.

### Added

- **The board's handed-over list shows only work this PC can take.** A request
  the board routed to someone else (devin, muse, owner, hold, ...) is no longer
  listed; one for `local-claude` is listed when `local_taker` is set up, and a
  session started for it takes the request with that writer's key.
- **Run work the board's owner handed to this PC, unattended.** With
  `local_taker` in `board.json`, the Hub looks at the board every few minutes
  and takes a request for `local-claude` that the owner handed over and routed
  from the board page, runs it with `claude -p` (an Anthropic API key from an
  env file, the title on stdin as data, in the project's listed folder), and
  writes the start, a short masked result and `done` (or the reason and
  `waiting`) onto the item. One run at a time, a daily cap and a timeout. Work a
  writer handed over or routed is never run. See `docs/manual_board-sync.md`.
- **Open files on an ssh host without any setup.** When a shell session was
  started as `ssh -i <key> user@host`, right-clicking an absolute path (`/…` or
  `~/…`) in the terminal now offers "Open from user@host" (read-only modal) and
  "Fetch" — no attachment destination needs to be set first. It is read-only and
  never changes where attachments are sent. Connections that use `-p`, `-J`, `-F`
  or `-l` are not detected; set the destination by hand for those.
- **Start work the board's owner handed over.** When the owner of an MCP board
  (for example Many Iris) hands a piece of planned work to an AI, the Hub's
  sidebar shows "Work handed over from the board" for the projects listed in
  `board.json`. Choosing one opens the ordinary new-session form with the
  project's folder and the work's title filled in; nothing starts until you
  press Launch. The session then takes the request on the board
  (`board_accept_handoff`), and its start, summaries and end are written onto
  the handed-over item instead of a new `session/<id>` item. A request someone
  else took first leaves the session an ordinary one. See
  `docs/manual_board-sync.md`.- **A commit named in a finished-work summary links to its GitHub page on the
  board.** When a summary has no `成果:` link but names a commit by its hash
  (7 or more characters, for example "pushed 0a1b2c3d"), and that commit is on
  a branch of `origin` on GitHub, the note on the board gets the commit's page
  as its link. A commit that is not pushed gets no link, and the repository's
  newest commit is never guessed: with several sessions in one repository it
  may be another session's work.
- **Input buttons live inside the progress band, and up to 10 quick commands.**
  On a wide screen the buttons stay in the band that shows the working message.
  Drag a button by its corner grip and drop it between others to reorder them
  (the others slide aside, as on a phone home screen); they can no longer be
  placed outside the band, and only the order is saved, so opening the sidebar
  or resizing the window no longer leaves them behind. Drag the divider between
  the message and the buttons to widen or narrow the button area (double-click
  to reset). Right-click anywhere on the band to list your quick commands: tick
  to show or hide a button (the command is kept), edit, delete, or add a new
  one, up to 10 (hidden ones count). The same list is in Settings. Your earlier

  are gone. Voice input now uses the browser's built-in recognition only, and
  Settings → Voice offers `OFF` or `Browser`. If you used Whisper, a leftover
  `~/.many-ai-cli/whisper/` is reported by `many-ai-cli doctor` and removed by
  `many-ai-cli uninstall`; `voice.whisper.*` keys in `config.yaml` are ignored.
- **The NVIDIA NIM route and the Jev rating are removed.** Settings no longer
  has the "NVIDIA NIM for OpenCode" and "Jev evaluation" sections, the model
  picker no longer lists an NVIDIA NIM group, and the `/api/nvidia-nim*` and
  `/api/jev/evaluate` routes are gone. The Hub makes no request to NVIDIA or
  TypeSafe any more. An existing `nvidia_nim` key in `config.yaml` is ignored,
  and a key saved earlier stays in `~/.many-ai-cli/secrets/nvidia_api_key`
  until you delete the file yourself.

- **Official AI CLI catalog import.** The Hub no longer serves
  `/api/provider-distributions/*`, and the note about it under
  Settings → AI CLI integrations is gone. The import never worked in a release:
  no signing keys were configured, so checking and accepting a catalog always
  returned 503. Your own provider definitions and their history are unchanged.
- **The "Attach to grid" option in New Session.** It was always disabled; the
  "Hub tab" and "Detached window" choices remain.
- **README descriptions of `hub.open_browser`.** The setting has never had an
  effect (only `serve --open` opens the browser). An existing value in
  `config.yaml` is still accepted and ignored.

### Security

- **Git settings in a folder you open no longer run programs while the Hub
  looks at it.** A folder's own `.git/config` (an unpacked archive, a shared
  folder, a file an AI CLI wrote) could name a hook (`hook.<name>.command`) or
  a filter driver (`filter.<name>.clean` with `.gitattributes`), and the Git
  the Hub runs on its own ran them with your permissions: the filter as soon
  as the dashboard showed the session, the hook at your first input. The
  Hub's own Git (branch and change counts, turn snapshots, the Review and Git
  views, session worktrees) now asks Git for those names first and switches
  each one off; if the names cannot be read, that Git command does not run.
  What you do yourself in the Git view (commit, fetch, pull, push) still runs
  with the repository's hooks and filters. In a repository that uses a filter
  such as Git LFS, the Hub's change counts and turn diffs now compare the
  files as they are on disk, so they can differ from `git status`.
- **Closing a session no longer fetches.** With
  `user_prefs.spawn.worktree_cleanup: delete`, closing a worktree session (and
  each Hub start) fetched the parent repository's upstream to see whether the
  branch was merged, and a fetch runs what the repository's config names (the
  remote's transport and upload-pack command, hooks on the updated refs).
  Cleanup now judges against the upstream as it was last fetched. After a
  merge on the remote, fetch from the Git view or your own Git, and the
  worktree is removed at the next check; until then it stays.
- **Auto-approval, batch approval and "add to auto-approval" act only on a
  shell command the Hub has confirmed.** Three ways an approval could be
  answered without you seeing what ran are closed:
  - *The hidden part of a command was not judged.* The Hub hides secret-looking
    values (`token=…`, `password=…`, `Bearer …`, known key prefixes) before it
    shows a command, and it also judged the command after hiding them. Text
    placed where the value goes, such as a pipe into another program or a
    `$(…)`, was therefore shown as `[REDACTED]` and never looked at: the
    command could be LOW, match a rule, share a batch with a different
    command, and be saved as a rule that matched any value. The risk is now
    judged before anything is hidden, and a command with a hidden part is never
    LOW.
  - *Some shell syntax made two commands look like one.* A quote the Hub
    counted differently from the shell (`$'…\'…'`, a `#` comment holding a
    quote), or a PowerShell `( … )` in an argument, let a second command sit
    behind a LOW first one. LOW is now given only to text made of constructs
    the Hub can split the way the shell does; a line break, `#`, `( ) { }`,
    `$'`, `$"`, `${`, a backslash before a quote, or an unclosed quote makes
    it MID. A rule never matches a command of several lines.
  - *A line that merely read like a command was taken as the command.* For a
    prompt without Claude Code's `Bash command` heading, the Hub took a line
    such as `Run: …` or `Command: …` from the 12 lines above the options, even
    when the prompt asked about something else (creating a file, a fetch, an
    MCP tool) and the line was the AI's own text. Such a prompt is now never
    LOW, and rules and batch approval do not act on it.

  What changes for you: auto-approval and batch approval now work for Claude
  Code's Bash prompts only (the command is checked against Claude Code's own
  record of the call). Prompts of the other CLIs, and commands that contain a
  secret-looking value, parentheses, braces, a comment or several lines, wait
  for you; you can still answer them from the dashboard or a notification.
- **Text the Hub types on its own no longer answers an approval prompt.**
  When the Hub types into an AI session by itself, it pastes the text and
  presses Enter. If the session was showing an approval prompt at that moment,
  the Enter answered the prompt for you. Relay reminders and conductor notices
  were already held back while a prompt was open; these were not, and now are:
  - the notice a parent gets when a child's launch instructions could not be
    delivered (held, and typed once the parent has moved on);
  - the request for a handoff note and the request for a turn summary (typed
    once the prompt is gone; a note request that cannot be typed within a
    minute is reported as "not written");
  - the request for an AI-written commit message from the Git view (refused
    with a message while the session waits on an approval);
  - `many-ai-cli orchestrate send` and the `inject` API (refused with HTTP 409
    `session_waiting_approval`, or `session_not_ready` while the session is
    starting, reconnecting or has queued input; nothing is typed, and the
    caller sends again later). An `inject` with `interrupt` no longer sends
    its ESC to a prompt either.

  Two cases where the Hub did not notice the prompt are closed as well. After
  you answered a Claude Code Bash prompt from the Hub, a second command whose
  first line was the same (a heredoc `git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF'`, for
  example) was taken for the prompt you had just answered: no approval card
  appeared, and the session did not count as waiting. Every line of the command
  now tells two prompts apart. And a prompt that is on the screen now holds
  the Hub's own typing back even when no approval card was opened for it.
- **A relay can no longer skip the PIN.** With a PIN set, a connection counts
  as local only when it proves it: the dashboard the Hub opened itself carries
  a cookie it got with its launch code, and the many-ai-cli commands on this
  machine (and the usage relay and `orchestrate` inside sessions) send a proof
  made from the private config. The launcher fetches the remote proof over
  SSH. Everything else, including a hand-typed `127.0.0.1` address and
  connections through socat, a reverse proxy or `ssh -L`, is asked for the PIN.
  Before, the Hub judged by the Host and proxy headers, which a relay passes
  through unchanged.
- **The token is no longer kept in a cookie.** A browser sends a 127.0.0.1
  cookie to every port on 127.0.0.1, so another program listening there could
  receive it. The dashboard now sends the token in a header and in the first
  WebSocket message only. Images, video, audio and downloads, which cannot
  carry a header, use a read-only ticket that works only for those reads, lasts
  12 hours and ends when the token is rotated. The dashboard page itself is
  served without the token; a browser that holds no token is told how to sign
  in. A token cookie left by an earlier version is deleted.
- **The browser is opened with a one-time code, not the token.** When the
  Hub, the CLI, the tray or the launcher opens the dashboard, the browser's
  command line (which other users of a Linux or macOS machine can read)
  carries a code that works once, for one minute, and only for a connection
  opened by the Hub's own OS user. The dashboard trades it for the token on
  the sign-in page and removes it from the address bar. The launcher's own
  settings screen still opens with its own token.
- **What the launcher hands to the browser is of no use to another user of the
  machine.** Two things another OS user of the machine the launcher runs on
  could take from the browser's command line are closed:
  - *The one-time code of a Hub behind SSH.* With `many-ai-cli connect
    --profile`, `many-ai-cli-launcher -profile` or `-last` and an SSH profile,
    the code went on the browser's command line. A Hub behind an SSH forward
    cannot tell who connected to the local end of the forward, so another user
    could use the code first and receive the remote Hub's token. The launcher
    now starts the browser on a one-time page of its own, answers that page
    only for a connection opened by the launcher's OS user, and sends the
    browser on to the Hub from there; the code is asked for when the browser
    arrives and never appears on a command line. If the browser does not ask
    for the page within 30 seconds, the launcher says so and the connection
    stays up; run the command again to open the dashboard.
  - *The token of the launcher's settings screen.* It is still in the address
    the browser is started with, but the screen now answers only connections
    opened by the launcher's OS user. Anyone else who has the address gets
    `403` for the page and for every request, so they can no longer rewrite
    profiles (and so run commands over your SSH) or read the address of a
    connected Hub.

  Where the launcher cannot find out who opened a connection (an OS other than
  Windows, Linux and macOS, or a browser that reaches the launcher through
  another user's process), the page and the settings screen answer nobody.
- **On the computer the Hub runs on, the browser keeps the sign-in only until
  the tab is closed.** The dashboard kept the Hub token in the browser's
  storage for `http://127.0.0.1:<port>`, so that a bookmark could open it
  again. A browser keeps that storage per address, port included, and does not
  know who answers there: while the Hub was stopped, or after it started on
  another port because its own was taken, another user of the same computer
  could listen on the port, and a page they served could read the token. A
  desktop browser on `127.0.0.1` / `localhost` now keeps the token and the
  read-only ticket in the tab only, and the service worker keeps no token
  there.
  - Reloading, and reconnecting after the Hub restarts, work as before, and so
    do the windows the dashboard opens itself. A new tab, a bookmark or the
    installed app shows "not signed in": open the dashboard from many-ai-cli
    (or the tray), which hands the token over with a one-time code each time.
  - A token an earlier version left in the browser is moved into the tab and
    deleted the first time the updated dashboard opens.
  - Phones and tablets (including a phone that opens its own `127.0.0.1`
    through an SSH forward), and addresses other than `127.0.0.1`, keep the
    sign-in as before, so the home-screen app still opens.
  - What remains: a tab that is still open holds the token, so reloading that
    tab while another program answers on the port still hands it over.
  - A Hub that could not have its configured port now says so when it starts
    (in its terminal and in the log): the old address reaches whoever holds
    that port.
- **The cookie that lets a browser the Hub opened skip the PIN ends when it
  should.** A browser sends a `127.0.0.1` cookie to every port, and this one
  was valid for 30 days on its signature alone: logging out and changing the
  PIN did not end it. It now counts only while the Hub remembers handing it
  out, to a browser that looks the same, for 7 days. Logging out, changing or
  clearing the PIN, revoking all access and restarting the Hub each end it.
  With a PIN set, a tab left open across a Hub restart is asked for the PIN
  (or open the dashboard again from many-ai-cli).
- **"Open in terminal" starts the terminal only on a folder that exists, and
  looks at nothing on another machine.** The path comes from a link: text an
  AI CLI printed, a file name, a link in a Markdown file.
  - The text was handed to the terminal app as it was. A folder name that did
    not exist could carry a `;`, which Windows Terminal (when set as
    `terminal_app`) reads as the start of another command; a path to a file
    (a work-memo path without an extension counts as a folder) could reach the
    macOS or Linux terminal app, which may run it. The Hub now resolves the
    path and starts the terminal on an existing folder only: the folder
    itself, or the folder of an existing file. A name that does not exist
    answers "folder not found". A configured Windows Terminal (`wt`,
    `wt.exe`, `WindowsTerminal.exe`) gets the folder as `-d` with each `;`
    escaped, like the default one.
  - On Windows, a link spelled `\\host\share\…` made the Hub look the path up,
    and Windows connected to that host to do so (which can hand over a
    challenge-response of your sign-in). Such a spelling is now refused before
    anything looks at it. A folder on a network share can therefore no longer
    be opened in a terminal from the dashboard, as with "Open folder".
- **A connection from another machine cannot register itself as a session.**
  The sockets of running sessions are kept when access is revoked, so that
  work goes on. Someone who held the token (and a PIN session) remotely could
  open such a socket, and it stayed after "Revoke all access", a PIN change
  and logout: a session of theirs in your list, receiving what you typed into
  it. A session socket is now taken only from this machine (with a PIN set,
  only with the proof many-ai-cli makes from the private config).
- **Request bodies have a size that fits and a time limit.** The request that
  trades a launch code is read before any credential is checked; it accepted
  up to 1 MiB with no time limit, so anyone who could reach the port could
  hold connections and memory. It now takes 1 KiB within 10 seconds, and a
  request from another machine is answered before its body is read. Every
  other request body must arrive within 30 seconds (10 minutes for uploads);
  a body that takes longer gets `408`.
- **The progress board (`board.json`) hands its key and a plan's title to
  less.** Two things the Hub sent on its own are narrowed:
  - *The key of a board on this machine.* With a board address of
    `http://127.0.0.1…` (or `localhost`, `[::1]`), the Hub sent the board's
    write key to whoever listened on that port; while the board server was
    stopped, another user of the machine could take the port and receive the
    key within a minute. The Hub now sends it only when every listener on the
    port belongs to your own OS user, does not read the key file otherwise,
    and never sends such a request through a proxy. A board server that runs
    as a different OS user on the same machine is therefore no longer written
    to; use an `https` address for it.
  - *The title of a plan.* A summary that names a plan file (`計画: <path>`)
    makes the Hub read that file's first heading as the title of a new board
    item. A link in the repository named like a plan could lead to
    any file on the machine, whose first `#` line was then sent to the board.
    The title is now read only from a Markdown file that is really inside the
    repository once links are resolved.
- **Release keys wait for the owner's approval.** The npm and Homebrew/winget
  publishing jobs use the `release` environment, so the keys they need are
  handed over only after the owner approves the run (one approval covers
  both).
- **npm packages are published without a stored npm key.** The release
  publishes to npm through npm's Trusted Publishing, which accepts only this
  repository's release workflow running in the approved `release` environment.
  There is no long-lived npm key left to leak or to expire. The workflow only
  stages each version; it goes live when the owner approves it on npmjs.com
  with two-factor authentication.
- **The CLI sends the Hub token only to a Hub that runs as you.** Before
  `status`, `stop`, a wrapped session, the usage relay, `orchestrate`, the
  tray and the launcher send the token to a 127.0.0.1 port, they ask the
  system whether that port's listener (for a wrapped session: the far end of
  the connection itself) belongs to your OS user. On a shared machine another
  user who took the port first no longer receives the token, the terminal
  output or a way to type into your session. The Hub's own startup check also
  reads its `/api/info` answer only up to 1 MiB.
- **You are told when wrong PINs lock PIN entry.** When five wrong PINs in a
  row lock one source, or many wrong PINs lock PIN entry for everyone, the
  security notification (ntfy and push) says where the attempts came from and
  for how long entry is locked. A right PIN on the attempt that reaches the
  limit leaves no lock, so it sends nothing.
- **The ntfy settings now say what the approval buttons can do.** Approve and
  Reject in an ntfy approval notification answer without the Hub token or PIN
  for 120 seconds, so the settings screen tells you not to let others see your
  notifications, and that an http destination gets only the Open button.
- **A repository can no longer loosen a bounded Claude child's sandbox.**
  Claude Code adds a project's own sandbox lists to the session's, so a
  `.claude/settings.json` in the repository could let the child's commands
  skip the sandbox, write outside the folder or reach the network. When the
  project settings between the working folder and its Git root widen the
  sandbox, the bounded Claude child is not started and the reason is shown.
- **A bounded OpenCode child is shown as full access.** OpenCode's unattended
  mode runs any command its deny rules do not name, so asking for `bounded`
  now starts it as `full` and the confirmation dialog says so, as for Grok and
  Cursor Agent.
- **CI and release builds use Bun 1.4.4.** Bun 1.3.14 was affected by three
  advisories fixed in 1.4.4, including the brotli decoder flaw that CISA lists
  as known exploited (CVE-2026-111497). The release jobs run `bun install` with
  Bun before building the web assets embedded in every binary, so the pinned
  version, the toolchain checks and the README toolchain table move to 1.4.4.
  `web/bun.lock` is unchanged.
- **Approvals are decided on the whole Bash command.** Claude shows a Bash
  permission as a heading, the command and its description, and many-ai-cli
  read only the first line under the heading. A second line was never
  classified, so an automatic rule written for the first line, "Approve all"
  or a one-tap link could approve it. The Hub now takes the exact command from
  Claude's transcript, which Claude writes before showing the prompt, and
  classifies and matches all of it. When the command cannot be confirmed, its
  risk shows at least as medium and only an answer on the prompt itself
  approves it.
- **`git difftool` is never low risk.** Treating `git diff` as a prefix also
  rated `git difftool -x <program>` as low; low-risk prefixes now end at a word
  boundary (so `lsof` and `dirname` are no longer low either), and
  `git difftool` always needs a person's confirmation.
- **Relay and orchestration text never answers a waiting prompt.** With a relay
  role set to Attended, a child that waited on an approval with no output for
  the idle threshold could get the relay reminder, whose Enter selects the
  focused "Yes"; relay instructions and notices to the session that started a
  relay or to a conductor were typed the same way. These texts are now typed
  only while the session waits on nothing. Otherwise they are held and typed
  once it can take them, and an approval opening between the pasted text and
  its Enter stops the Enter. Time spent waiting on an approval no longer counts
  toward the reminder or the child timeout. A held relay instruction is kept in
  the relay record, so it survives a Hub restart.
- **Opening a folder no longer runs programs its `.git` names.** A folder you
  open may hold a `.git` someone else wrote (an unpacked archive, a shared
  folder). The Git that many-ai-cli runs on its own there (the branch and
  change count, turn snapshots, the Review and Git tabs, `doctor`) followed
  that repository's config, so its fsmonitor hook, hooks such as
  `post-index-change`, and diff or textconv drivers could run as you, without
  any action. It now runs with the fsmonitor and hooks off, without external
  diff or textconv, and without signature checks in `log`. Worktrees that
  many-ai-cli creates for a session no longer run the repository's
  `post-checkout` hook either. Commit, fetch, pull and push from the Git tab are
  your own actions and still run the repository's hooks, such as pre-commit.
  Filter drivers (`filter.<name>.clean`) are not covered yet.
- **"Open with default app" opens documents, media and text only.** A path in
  an AI's output or in a Markdown link could name a script, written so that it
  passed the check of executable types (`notes.bat\x\..`) or of a type that
  check did not list (`.sh`, `.jar`, `.chm`), and the operating system ran it
  through the file's association. The path is now resolved once and the type
  is judged on the resolved name, which is also what is opened: PDF, Office
  documents that cannot hold macros, images, audio, video, and the text and
  source files the Hub can preview open in their app; any other file is
  selected in its folder instead, with a notice. Spellings that Windows
  rewrites before opening (a trailing dot or space, `name:stream`, a final `.`
  or `..`) and network or device paths (`\\server\share`) are refused. "Open
  folder" hands the system an existing folder only, and on macOS a folder that
  can be an application (`Name.app`) is only selected in Finder.
- **"Open in terminal" keeps a `;` in the folder name.** Windows Terminal reads
  a `;` as the start of another command even inside the folder argument, so a
  folder named `build;<command>` could start that command in a new tab. Each
  `;` is now escaped as Windows Terminal expects. Explorer's command line uses
  commas as separators, so folder paths are now passed to it in quotes.
- **A provider that is not installed no longer runs a file of its name from the
  project folder.** When a provider's command was not found on PATH, its bare
  name was passed on, and Windows looks for such a name in the session's
  folder first, so a repository carrying a file named `claude` (no extension
  needed) ran it as you when you started that provider there. A command that
  cannot be found is now an error on every OS, including custom providers and
  `copilot` when neither `copilot` nor `gh` is found: the session ends with
  "not found in PATH" as before, and nothing from the folder starts.
- **The Hub token is no longer written into the status line and usage hook
  commands.** The Claude Code status line and the Codex Stop hook that
  many-ai-cli sets up started with `MANY_AI_CLI_HUB_TOKEN=<token>`, and the AI
  CLI runs them through a shell, whose command line other users of the same
  Linux or macOS machine may read in the process list. The token now stays in
  the environment the AI CLI inherits from many-ai-cli, which the usage relay
  already read first. A Codex started outside many-ai-cli while the hook is in
  place no longer reports its usage to a many-ai-cli session. Hooks written by
  earlier versions are still recognized and replaced.
- **Another HTTPS port of the Hub's machine name is no longer trusted.** With
  remote access on (the machine name in `allowed_hosts`, as the mobile
  connection wizard sets it up), the Hub took any `https://` page on that name
  as its own dashboard, whatever its port. A script on another HTTPS service of
  the same machine could then open the dashboard's WebSocket with your cookies
  and type into sessions. An https origin must now match the host and port the
  request was sent to; `tailscale serve` keeps working as before.
- **The npm command starts the platform executable only from its own
  installation.** The `many-ai-cli` command installed with npm, pnpm or bun
  found the platform package the way Node finds modules, which goes on to every
  `node_modules` folder up to the drive root and to `NODE_PATH`. When the
  platform package was missing or incomplete (optional dependencies turned off,
  a failed download, an antivirus quarantine), it started a
  `C:\node_modules\many-ai-cli-windows-x64\bin\many-ai-cli.exe` that another
  user of the same Windows machine can create. It now looks only inside the
  installation that holds the command, checks that the package's name and
  version match, and otherwise stops with the "not installed" message as
  before, now naming what it found. A platform package supplied through
  `NODE_PATH` or a `node_modules` folder above the installation is no longer
  used.
- **The file view no longer reaches out to network shares.** The file
  content, image, download and list requests resolved any absolute path before
  checking where it was, including `\\server\share` and `//server/share`, and
  on Windows resolving such a path makes the system sign in to that server with
  your account. A web page you visited, or an image in Markdown you previewed in
  the Hub, could send that request. Network share and device paths are now
  refused before anything is opened; local paths, including the `\\?\C:\`
  spelling, work as before.
- **ntfy approval buttons are sent only to an https ntfy server.** The
  Approve and Reject buttons in an ntfy notification answer the prompt without
  the Hub token or PIN for 120 seconds, and they were sent to `http` ntfy
  servers too, where anyone on the network path could read or swap them. With
  an `http` server the notification now carries only Open. Notifications no
  longer follow redirects, which could hand them to another host.
- **Sockets without a token can no longer keep sessions from connecting.**
  Anyone who could reach the Hub's port, including another user of the same
  machine, could hold all 64 places for WebSocket connections that have not
  yet authenticated, reopening each within its 10 seconds, without the token.
  New AI CLI sessions then failed to register, the dashboard could not
  reconnect, and after a Hub restart running sessions could not reattach.
  Connections that present the Hub token when they open (the wrapper now sends
  it in a header; the dashboard sends its token cookie) wait in a separate
  pool that such sockets cannot fill. The token is still checked in the first
  message as before.
- **PIN guessing through a proxy that does not name the user is slowed down.**
  Remote PIN attempts that came through a proxy without a Tailscale user name
  met only the global limit (30 failures, then 60 seconds), about 40,000
  guesses a day. They now share one lock that grows from 60 seconds to 5 and
  30 minutes, the global lock grows the same way, and both start over after an
  hour without attempts.
- **Release signing no longer covers bytes the SBOM tool could change.** Syft
  ran in the job that also wrote the checksum file the release signs, after the
  payload had been checked, so a replaced Syft or installer could swap a ZIP or
  package and still get it signed. Syft now comes from its release tarball
  checked against a pinned SHA-256 and runs in a job of its own; the payload
  digests are recorded before it runs, and the checksum file is written and
  signed only for the recorded payload.
- **The release gate counts only pushes to this repository.** The check that
  validation and scans passed for the tag commit also took pull-request runs,
  which anyone can open at that commit: a fork's run could block a release or
  hide a failed push run. It now judges push runs on `main`, `develop`,
  `release/*`, `hotfix/*` and the tag, and a branch push run must pass as well
  as the tag's own.
- **A worktree is never created through a link in the repository.** A
  repository could commit `.git-worktrees` or `.many-ai-cli` as a link to a
  folder elsewhere; a session started with its own worktree, or a child
  started by a conductor, then checked the repository's files out there,
  without an approval. The worktree folders are now made one level at a time
  below the repository, a link or junction at any of those levels stops the
  worktree, and a repository that tracks `.git-worktrees` gets none. Links
  above the repository folder still work.
- **The board sync reads at most 1 MiB of a reply.** Writing to an MCP board
  read the whole reply into memory, so a board that answered with gigabytes
  (a compromised server, or another program on a loopback port the board was
  not yet using) could exhaust the Hub's memory at each session start, turn
  and end. A reply declared or found to be longer than 1 MiB is now dropped
  with a warning.
- **On Windows the history database stays private in any log folder.** With
  `hub.log_dir` in a folder other users can change (a new folder at the root
  of a data drive gives every signed-in user that right), SQLite created the
  database's `-wal` and `-shm` files with the folder's permissions, so another
  user could read recent history or alter it, and a database file another
  user placed there was used as is. Before SQLite opens them, the database,
  `-wal` and `-shm` now get the same user-only permissions as the database,
  and a file that belongs to another user stops the history from opening.
- **Claude's per-session settings no longer go to the shared temporary
  folder.** The wrapper wrote the status line and delegation files under a
  predictable name in the system temporary folder, so on Linux another user
  could take that name first, or leave any file whose name is not UTF-8, and
  Claude then started without them. They are now written to
  `~/.many-ai-cli/tmp` (user-only) under a name with a random part, and a
  failed look for old files no longer stops the new one.
- **The bounded tier now limits what an allowed command runs.** A bounded
  child could edit a test or a package script and then run it through
  `go test` or `bun run check` from the built-in list, so code the child wrote
  ran with your rights and could do what the list leaves out. On macOS, Linux
  and WSL2 a bounded Claude child now runs its shell commands in Claude Code's
  sandbox: they write only in its working folder and cannot reach the
  network, and Go builds use a build cache of the session's own. On Linux and
  WSL2 the sandbox needs bubblewrap and socat; without them Claude Code
  refuses to start the child. Without a sandbox (Claude on native Windows,
  and Copilot) the built-in list keeps reading, editing, `git add` and
  `git commit`, and the child's Git commands run no repository hooks; Claude
  still runs the read-only forms of `git status`, `git diff` and `git log`,
  and Copilot asks you about anything else. Claude's file tools stay in the
  working folders everywhere.
- **A crafted skill can no longer keep the Hub busy while it reads YAML.**
  The decoder counted each expansion of a YAML merge as one step whatever it
  copied, so a SKILL.md front matter with a long key merged many times took
  seconds to minutes of CPU time each time the slash commands were listed.
  A mapping that merges name is now resolved once, and the budget counts the
  bytes each step copies, so such a file decodes quickly or stops at the
  limit.
- **Default usage links fetched from GitHub are used only when they are https
  URLs.** The settings screen takes the default "usage page" links for each
  provider from this project's `resources/` on GitHub and opens them when you
  click. A value with another scheme (`javascript:`, a custom app scheme,
  `http:`) is now dropped by the Hub and again by the screen, and the built-in
  default is used instead. Links you enter yourself are not affected.
- **The bundled SQLite is updated to a version with the fix for
  RUSTSEC-2026-0459 (CVE-2026-119375).** `rusqlite` goes from 0.40.2 to 0.41.1
  (`libsqlite3-sys` 0.38.2 to 0.39.1). The flaw is in reading a crafted `-wal`
  file placed beside a database the Hub opens; the Hub's databases are created
  by the Hub in its own folder.
- **Release workflow: reruns, release notes and the token check are bound to
  the tag.** A channel rerun (npm, Homebrew, winget) started from a branch ran
  that branch's scripts with the publishing token and npm's signing identity
  once approved; every manual run must now start at the tag, each job checks
  out the tag commit, and the `release` environment accepts only `v*` tags.
  The text of a GitHub Release was passed between jobs as a file that a later
  job could replace; it is now written from the tag's CHANGELOG by the job
  that publishes it. The check of the publishing token's scopes had stopped
  running after the token moved into the `release` environment; it now runs
  inside that environment, right before the token is used.
- **The npm launcher now requires Node.js 22 or later** (`engines.node` was
  `>=18`; Node.js 18 and 20 no longer receive security fixes). CI and the
  release workflow build with Node.js 22.23.5 (2026-11-11) and 24.22.3
  (2026-11-10), the current security releases.

- **A start-failure note no longer copies secrets from the child's screen.**
  When a child session fails to start, the Hub writes the last lines of its
  screen to the orchestration board and to the parent session. A token printed
  there was stored as it appeared; those lines are now masked like the rest of
  the stored text.

- **The re-sign-in page returns only to a path on this Hub.** A signed-out
  browser that still held a valid token could be sent to another site by a link
  such as `http://127.0.0.1:<port>//example.invalid/`. The token was not sent
  (the referrer policy blocks it), and the page now returns to `/` in that case.

- **The security notes in the README now say what the token allows.** It gives
  full control of the Hub, it is passed to every AI CLI the Hub starts, and it
  can appear on process command lines, so the Hub is meant for a machine only
  you use. The notes also say that Git runs in each session's folder.

- **The `crypto-bigint` library behind the Web Push signature is updated to
  0.7.10.** The version we shipped, 0.7.8, had been withdrawn (yanked) from the
  crates.io registry. No security advisory is attached to it; this keeps the
  build on a published version, so the dependency audit now reports no warning.

- **The pre-v1 GHCR container images were deleted (2026-10-25).** All tags of
  `ghcr.io/ishizakahiroshi/many-ai-cli` bundled a Node.js 22 release affected by the
  Brotli decoder vulnerability CVE-2026-111497, and image publishing has stopped,
  so they would never receive the fix. Use the Linux binary instead.
